title.narrative: People-centered Smart Cities Flagship Programme - Digital Governance in Cities

description.narrative: The recent advances in digital technologies – from the internet of things and artificial intelligence to digital platforms for service delivery and 5G for autonomous mobility – are rapidly transforming societies and advancing the capabilities of local governments to deliver services in the digital word. As the world grapples with the COVID-19 pandemic, it is witnessing first-hand how these digital technologies help to confront the threat and keep people connected. Both governments and societies are relying on these technologies to continue deliver government services, enable education, work and economic activities to continue and at the same time to stay connected with family and friends. Many new technologies have “transformed public governance and provided new possibilities for citizens, policymakers, and public managers to rethink how public services should be planned, designed, delivered, monitored, and evaluated”. The growing use of these digital technologies have also sparked the debate about how they should be regulated and managed, what values and principles should guide their use, and the role of local governments in ensuring digital technologies are appropriately deployed, their risks mitigated and their potential harnessed for the benefit of all. Issues of digital inclusion and digital human rights – how digital technology affects existing human rights – are emerging as critical as intelligent systems and data intensive technologies can reinforce existing biases and discrimination and also make it easier for easier for public and private sector organizations to track, analyze, predict and to some degree manipulate people’s behaviors. The UN Secretary-General’s Roadmap on Digital Cooperation highlights key concerns in the areas of data protection, digital identity, the use of surveillance technologies, online harassment and content governance and calls for the redoubling of efforts to better harness the potential of digital technologies while mitigating the harm that they may cause . The UN Strategy on Sustainable Urban Development highlights digital transformation and new technologies as one of four frontier issues that require a special, coordinated response. In the New Urban Agenda, Member States committed to “adopting a smart-city approach that makes use of opportunities from digitalization, clean energy and technologies, as well as innovative transport technologies” . In response to the Member States’ commitments, UN-Habitat’s People-Centered Smart Cities flagship programme supports national and local governments with their digital transition, applying a multi-level governance strategy to help build skills and capabilities to develop, procure and effectively use digital technologies in an ethical and inclusive way to make sure that no one is left behind . Legislations, policies and guidelines, and governance structures at the national and local level are needed to safeguard data, address the digital divide and promote digital inclusion of people with specific needs and other vulnerable groups. Effective due diligence is required to ensure that technology solutions, policies, practices and terms of service comply with human rights principles and standards. Local governments can play an important role in countering the challenges and risks of rising digitalization in public service delivery and implications such as digital divide, digital inclusion, and social equity. Through digital governance, which can be defined as “a framework for establishing accountability, roles and decision making for an organization’s digital presence” and for managing the ethical concerns associated with digital technologies, local governments can fundamentally change how they operate, engage citizens and achieve efficiency and cost-effectiveness while leaving no one behind and no one offline. However, digital governance is a new topic to many local governments and there is often a significant mismatch between their capabilities and that of the big technology firms that they often procure technology from and/or contract them for deploying new technologies. Many cities don’t have the appropriate digital governance structures and other mechanisms in place to deal with these rising issues. The topic of digital governance in cities is increasingly being raised by Member States, partner organizations, UN agencies, city networks and private companies as something that needs additional and special attention. The project seeks to address the growing concerns related digital human rights and broader issues of digital governance including digital inclusion and digital divide by providing guidance to local government authorities on how overcome digital governance challenges and institute governance measures and establish digital governance structures.
